Not verified: layoff headcounts precisely (sources range 30-40%), anything Meyer says in her own voice. Year empty. UPDATE: Pure Atria fact removed. Layoff headcount left vague because sources conflict (a third of 120 vs a third leaving 120). UPDATE: sajithpai.com and mickmel.substack.com book notes (keeper test, severance 4-9 months, top-of-market pay, earlier expense wording). Blog reviews, not book text.
facts: After the dot-com crash dried up venture capital in 2001, Hastings laid off about a third of Netflix's staff, including some who were doing adequate work (sources disagree on the headcount).
Hastings expected morale and output to fall; instead those who stayed were more productive and the company worked better. He draws from it the idea of talent density.
In 2003 an employee questioned the vacation policy and Hastings removed it; Netflix has since neither allotted vacation days nor tracked days off.
Leaders were expected to take long vacations openly; example guardrails: no vacation within two weeks of a deadline, two weeks' notice for a five-day vacation.
Employees did not take much more time off than under the old policy.
The expense policy became five words: act in Netflix's best interest, reportedly reworked from spend company money as if it were your own after people grew too frugal (summary, not book text).
Hastings says freedom works only when talent density is high and feedback is candid.

The expense policy example: economy class unless an employee must present at an early-morning conference after a redeye, when business class is justified. Safeguards: managers regularly sample expenses, employees know they could be checked at any time, and managers tell staff when someone is fired for overspending (shortform.com/blog/no-rules-rules-book).

The keeper test: managers ask whether they would fight to keep an employee who said they were leaving for a similar job at a peer company; if not, Netflix lets the person go with a severance of about four to nine months (blog reviews). Netflix pays top of the market for each role and has no bonuses.
The expense policy replaced an earlier wording, spend company money as if it were your own, which led people to be too frugal (blog review).
The book treats staying silent when you have useful feedback as disloyal to the company.
scene_details: a company of about 120 after a layoff
a vacation policy with no tracking
an expense policy of five words
tension: Netflix cut a third of its staff and got better results, then took rules away.
opening_idea: Open on the five-word expense policy or the day after the 2001 layoff.

lessons.idea: A rule is often a patch for someone you do not trust; before adding one, check whether the person or the information is the actual gap.
lessons.anchor: five words replacing an expense policy

reflect_final: Which rule in your team or home exists because of one person or one incident, and what would you check before keeping it?

use_cases.situation: Someone proposes a new approval step after one mistake.
use_cases.move: Ask what the one mistake was and whether a conversation would fix it.

use_cases.situation: You manage a person who wants more freedom.
use_cases.move: Offer one decision they own fully, and agree how you will give feedback on it.

use_cases.situation: A household chore system keeps failing.
use_cases.move: Drop one rule for two weeks and see who notices.

pocket_idea: Five words replaced a whole expense policy; ask what a rule is covering for.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Netflix's expense policy is five words long.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: After the 2001 crash, Netflix laid off about a third of its people. Hastings expected the rest to slump and they did better. He later removed the vacation policy and replaced expense rules with five words: act in Netflix's best interest.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Which rule do you keep without knowing why?
